segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We've seen quite a few prepositions up until now, these words

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: that refer to movement, or position, or direction.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, we had two words for "for", what were they?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Para and por.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Para and por. And how did we say "from" or "of"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: De.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: De. "With"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Con.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Con. "In" or "on"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: En.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: En. Good. So we've seen quite a few of those.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, prepositions in Spanish won't come at the end of the sentence as they can in English.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We've seen this already as well. Do you remember how to say "Where are you from?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "You are", speaking informally from ser, is eres. Eres.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "Where are you from?"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿De dónde eres?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿De dónde eres? So in English, "Where are you from?", we're putting the preposition at the end of the sentence and that's fine in English, but it's incorrect Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you don't say "where are you from?", you say "from where are you?": ¿De dónde eres?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If we want to say "where are you going?" in Spanish, we say "to where are you going?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "you are going" speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vas. Good. So, "To where are you going?"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Adónde vas?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Adónde vas? Good. "We are going to the United States."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The United States is Estados Unidos. United States, Estados Unidos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And I should mention you don't translate the word for "the", you just say "we are going to United States".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vamos a Estados Unidos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vamos a Estados Unidos. We discussed the concept before about working backwards.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So instead of building up to say what we want to say, finding bits of language and working backwards to find the "to" form of a verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for example, imagine we looked up somewhere "United States", or we asked somebody how to say "United States" and we came across Estados Unidos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can use unidos to work backwards to work out what is the verb "to unite". How do you think that is?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Unidar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Not guessing, but really working backwards, which instead of building up, building down. Instead of adding bits on to the verb, seeing what has been added and consciously taking it off.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, so -ido has been added. When you add -ido, you take off the ending of the "to" form.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And what is the ending with -ido?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: -ir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Or?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: -er.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You should experiment and see which one feels more natural to you. Now the one that you may have heard before is probably going to feel more natural even if you didn't register it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you heard before the correct version, it's going to feel more natural. And also the more words you learn in Spanish, the greater intuition you get about the phonetics of Spanish, what sounds more Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So that should direct you when you say uner, unir, uner, unir, to understand which one is "to unite". Which one do you think it is?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Somehow I think it's unir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Unir. But at this stage there is no reason for you to know what sounds more Spanish, huh? This intuition is something that occurs with practice and exposure and listening.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But working backwards is a useful skill that we want to employ in our language learning journey.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we said that prepositions won't come at the end. So if we say for example "the girl I work with",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: in Spanish, we will say "the girl with which, with that, with who I work". We have the option.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So what was "to work", do you remember?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Trabajo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Trabajar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Trabajar. "To work", good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "The girl" is la chica. La chica. It's kind of informal, but very common. La chica. How do you think "the guy" would be if "the girl" is la chica?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El chico.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El chico. So we can begin with the one that we know already which is "with that": con que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "The girl with that I work."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La chica con que yo trabajo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La chica con que trabajo. You don't need the yo unless you're emphasizing: la chica con que yo trabajo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We could also say "with which": la chica con cual trabajo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We could say "with who": la chica con quien trabajo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We could even put la que, or la cual, which means which, or that, but we're showing that it's a feminine which, or a feminine that. La chica con la cual trabajo. La chica con la que trabajo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You have all of those options in Spanish, but don't worry about them, you can just use que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So whilst you have all of those options and you will hear them, and when you get comfortable with hearing them and understanding them, you will start using the different ones without really thinking about it very much. You don't want to worry about it now. Que you can use for everything, for all of that.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La chica con que trabajo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So it's correct?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, it's correct Spanish, but you have all of those options: la chica con cual trabajo, la chica con la cual trabajo, la chica con la que trabajo, la chica con quien trabajo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "The girl that I was working with." So how would you say "it is, it is the girl I was working with"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Let's go through it slowly. "It is the girl"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es la chica...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ..."with who"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...con que...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...con que... "I was working", "I used to work".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So it's trabajar, and that becomes -aba, trabajaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Trabajaba. All together: "It's the girl I was working with."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es la chica con que trabajaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Es la chica con que trabajaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "the girl with whom, the girl that I was going to the party with"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "The girl with whom", or "with that", "with which", all of those are okay in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La chica con que...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La chica con que... "I was going to the party". So "I was going" is the line version of ir, which is irregular,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but we can remember that it takes a little bit from the two options that we have to make the line version. We have -aba for -ar verbs, and -ía for -er/-ir verbs, and the verb ir kind of blended together -aba and -ía and came up with...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...iba. Ah.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you can think of it that way, you can think of it like -aba and -ía kind of blending together to have iba, or you can think of it like the present, va, but with an "i" before.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In the past it's spelled with a "b", I-B-A, iba, whereas in the present it's spelled with a "v", V-A, but as we know they are very similar sounding.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So it's like the present with an "i" before.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in the present you have "he's going", él va, and then in the past él iba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So "I was going", "he was going", "she was going", "it was going", "you" (formal) "were going" is...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Iba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Iba. So, "The girl with which I was going to the party".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La chica con que iba a la fiesta.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. La chica con que iba a la fiesta. So you can say la chica con la cual, la chica con quien, la chica con la que, you have all of these options.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Let's use cuál in a sentence which is the word for "which". And it's not just a "which" like this to connect "the girl with which",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you can also use it like a question: "Which one do you want?" You probably can guess we don't need the word for "one".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Cuál quieres?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Which one do you want?": ¿Cuál quieres? Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So cuál, C-U-A-L, means "which".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I know" from saber, "to know", was sé. We said it's very irregular, just S-E, "I know".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sé.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say "I don't know which one he wants"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No sé cuál quiere.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No sé cuál quiere. How would you say "I don't know which one he wants to see"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No sé cuál quiere ver.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No sé cuál quiere ver. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now what if you wanted to say "I don't know with which one he wants to do it"? "I don't know which one he wants to do it with".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No sé con cuál quiere hacer... it with?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Well, you said the "with" already.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So it's just lo at the end.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, and you might feel this temptation often to repeat the preposition again at the end, even if you put it before, because that English is pushing through with the negative language transfer. No sé con cuál quiere hacerlo. "I don't know with which one he wants to do it", "I don't know which one he wants to do it with".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we don't put the preposition at the end of the sentence in Spanish, we will rearrange the sentence, and whilst this sounds more formal in English, of course it doesn't sound more formal in Spanish, it's just the only correct option.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "who", we've mentioned very briefly, is quién. Quién.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quién.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. If you want to say "who is going?", what verb version will "who" go with? Who is "who"? Is it "you", is it "them", is it "he/she/it"? Who is "who"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He/she/it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say "who is going?"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Quién va?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Quién va? Good. And in Spanish you have the plural of "who". If you're expecting more than one person, if you know that your "who" refers to more than one person, you can put quién into plural. So how do you think that would sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Quiénes?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, quiénes. So if you want to say "who's going?" and you know it's more than one person...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Quiénes van?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good! And you changed the verb as well to match: ¿quiénes van? Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "Who is here?"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Quién es aquí?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está, because it's estar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's your location.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Quién está aquí?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Quién está aquí? And if you knew you were talking about here, you could just leave that out. As we have the sense of location with estar, we don't really need to say "the here" if we know that we're talking about here.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Like we said before, if you knock on someone's door you just say ¿estás?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, right, yeah.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Because we're using estar and we're talking about states, that's enough context for us if we just leave it by itself to understand that we are speaking about location. So you could just say "Who is?"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Quién está?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Quién está?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I don't know with who I have to do it. I don't know who I have to do it with." How is "I have to"? What "have" do we use to get the meaning of "have to"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tengo... tener.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tener. Tener, "to have". "I have"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tengo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And to get the meaning of "I have to"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tengo que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo que. So, "I don't know who I have to do it with. I don't know with who I have to do it."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No sé con quién tengo que hacerlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No sé con quién tengo que hacerlo. Or if we knew we meant more than one person: no sé con quiénes tengo que hacerlo. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I don't know who I have to do it for. I don't know for who I have to do it."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No sé para quién tengo que hacerlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No sé para quién lo tengo que hacer, or no sé para quién tengo que hacerlo. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What if you wanted to say "I don't know who I have to do it because of. I don't know who I have to do it because of." So how would that sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No sé por quién tengo que hacerlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No sé por quién lo tengo que hacer. No sé por quién tengo que hacerlo.
